text:
Sooner or later, Sadiq Khan’s luck was bound to run out. Or was it? When he first stood for London mayor in 2016, the Tory candidate was Zac Goldsmith, who was accused of running a racist campaign. Not the brightest move in one of the most multicultural cities in Europe. Not to be outdone, four years later the Conservatives chose the completely anonymous Shaun Bailey. Even Shaun wasn’t sure who Shaun was. Especially when he was quite sure he could have sworn he wasn’t the Shaun Bailey who had an apparent Christmas party during lockdown, which he said “turned into something once I left”.
As if to prove it wasn’t an accident that they had previously fielded the worst candidates possible, the Tories came up with Susan Hall in 2024. A politician who makes Liz Truss look accomplished. Her campaign was one of the most joyous imaginable. A wild ride of one idiotic speech to the next. You kept thinking the Conservatives must be having a laugh and would unveil their serious candidate. Only they never did. The only votes she got were from those who had never heard her speak. The Tories would have done better if they had put up a turnip.
This time, the Tories are determined to take themselves a little more seriously. With the emphasis on a little. Enter James Cleverly. One of this column’s favourite sons. It’s only with his reappearance that you realise quite how much you’ve missed him. James has the CV of a political heavyweight. But at heart he still is, and always will be, Jimmy Dimly. The foreign secretary who rubbished Rishi Sunak’s Rwanda plan as “bat-shit crazy” only to find himself moved sideways to home secretary where he was forced to defend and implement it.
Things like this keep happening to Jimmy D. Disaster follows him around like an ultra-needy cockapoo. Yet you can’t help loving him for it. Because there’s something rather sweet about a man who takes himself quite so seriously. Never realising that the joke’s on him. People are laughing at him, not with him. A man who always seems to be living his life several sentences behind every conversation. Stuck in second gear. Someone who means well, but can’t quite keep up. We don’t know yet if Sadiq is planning to stand for a fourth term in 2028, but he may be looking at Dimly and thinking things could have been a lot worse.
Inside a central London office suite on Thursday morning, Jimmy D and the two other Tory mayoral candidates, Festus Akinbusoye and Sara Gezdari, gathered to hear the results of the first round of voting. Or only round. The returning officer announced that Dimly had received 86% of the vote and was duly elected. Interestingly, we weren’t told how many people had voted. I guess it’s less embarrassing than saying Jimmy had received 43 votes. Fair to say that this is not an election that has gripped the Tory party. Nor London. No one is much interested in who is going to be runner-up again to Labour.
Jimmy D gave a big smile. This was his moment and he was going to milk it. He strode to the lectern to address a largely uninterested audience. First, he wanted to thank Festus and Sara for the brilliant campaigns they had run and for the lively conversations they had sparked. “You are an asset to London and the whole country,” he said. Er … hang on a mo. What campaigns and what conversations? This was the first time most of London had heard of Festus and Sara, so it was tragic that the acclaim was for their imminent return to obscurity.
“Nobody loves London more than me,” Dimly continued. So he wasn’t planning to stand again as an MP. He was all in for London. This sounded more like a man clinging to a life raft than an endorsement of the capital. In truth, he has always looked out of sorts in Kemi Badenoch’s Reform-lite Conservative party. He had been more of an old-school Tory who was never comfortable just trashing foreigners and people on benefits. So this was more a last chance of extending his political career while maintaining some self-respect rather than a statement of commitment. He might be a bit crap, but he was a bit crap with a heart.
We then got five minutes of a love letter to London. “The answer to ‘why London’ is because London is London,” he said gnomically. At times like these, Dimly excels himself. We should treasure him while we still have him. London was the best city in the world. Then, as if realising he had just given a party broadcast on behalf of Sadiq, he gave us five minutes on why London was the most rubbish city in the world.
Basically everything that was wrong with London was the fault of “Khan”. Jimmy couldn’t bring himself to use his first name. Everywhere you went there were people being murdered in front of your eyes and motorists had been deprived of the opportunity of driving at high speed and killing cyclists and pedestrians. Only Dimly could make London a fun place again. To all those people who had been up all night playing Grand Theft Auto VI, he was going to turn the capital into a video game. London was going to be bigger than big. So big no one would ever miss it again. Or something.
There was just time for a few questions. How did he feel about having supported Truss’s mini-budget and being pro-Brexit? On the whole, Londoners weren’t that keen on either of these. Two-thirds of Londoners reckoned Brexit had been a disaster. How was he going to reconcile that one? Now Jimmy D struggled with his hearing. Turned out he couldn’t make out the Brexit word.
He didn’t want to talk about the past, he was the future. Except when he was talking about the Wrath of Khan. “Khan hates London,” he insisted. “What’s more Andy Burnham hates London too.” In the DimlyVerse, neither Sadiq nor Andy would be happy until the capital had been razed to the ground.
What about the commitment to abandoning net zero and membership of the ECHR? Those were Kemi’s red lines. Were they his? Jimmy shuffled awkwardly and mumbled “Yes”. A lie. Dimly believes in both. As do most Londoners. There has almost certainly been a pact that Kemi will look the other way so long as Jimmy doesn’t make a big deal about the differences in their politics.
Dimly just wanted to re-emphasise his commitment to London. He was all for the things that Londoners wanted. And if he wasn’t, he would do his best to pretend that he was. He couldn’t say fairer than that. “I am only going to comment on my comments,” he said in conclusion. Sometimes, it’s hard not to love him. At the very least, the next two years will be a golden time for sketch writers.
